summary: Describes a non-standard but widely implemented change to how TCP handles ICMP soft errors: pending connection attempts are rejected when such errors arrive. This avoids long delays, for example for dual-stack hosts with IPv6 enabled in mostly IPv4 networks. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: If you knock on a door and a sign says nobody lives here, give up quickly and try the next house. The TCP standard says the opposite: keep knocking for at least three minutes, because the sign may be out of date. Most stacks now give up straight away during connection setup, and this memo explains why and what it costs.

questions: how does tcp react to icmp soft errors
why does tcp abort on icmp destination unreachable
what is an icmp soft error
subtitle: Why many TCP stacks give up on a new connection at the first ICMP soft error, even though the standard says to keep trying.

tldr.problem: The TCP standard says a connection must not be abandoned when an ICMP soft error arrives, because such errors are usually transient. The result is that a host trying an unreachable address waits at least three minutes before moving on to the next one.
tldr.mechanism: Many stacks ignore the standard during connection setup and treat a soft error as a hard one in the SYN-SENT and SYN-RECEIVED states. A more careful version aborts only after a second error and several SYN retransmissions, using two new parameters.
tldr.outcome: The document records the widespread non-standard behaviour, its drawbacks and its small security cost, and states that it does not change the TCP standard.

facts.label: BSD abort rule
facts.value: Second ICMP error and more than three SYN retransmissions

today: RFC 5461 is an Informational document published in February 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents a non-standard behaviour and states that it does not change the TCP standard. The neighbouring problem of IPv6 hosts on a network with no IPv6 is described in RFC 4943.

sections.title: What the Document Is About
sections.content:
The handling of network failures splits into two actions. Fault isolation is what hosts and routers do to work out that there is a network failure, and fault recovery is what they do to try to survive it. In the Internet architecture, the Internet Control Message Protocol is one fault isolation technique for reporting network error conditions to the hosts sending datagrams.

When a host is notified of a network error, its network stack tries to continue communicating if it can, and the recovery strategy may depend on the type of failure and on when it was noticed. This document analyses the problems that can arise from TCP's recovery reactions to ICMP soft errors: the problems of a host trying to connect to a multihomed host with some unreachable addresses, and in particular the case of dual-stack nodes with IPv6 enabled by default deployed in IPv4 or mixed environments where the IPv6 connectivity does not exist.

Finally, the document documents a modification to TCP's reaction to ICMP soft errors during connection startup, implemented in a variety of TCP/IP stacks to overcome those problems. The document stresses that this modification runs contrary to standard behaviour and unambiguously does not change the standard reaction. The consensus of the TCP Maintenance and Minor Extensions Working Group was to document the widespread implementation of non-standard behaviour but not to change the TCP standard.
sections.plainLanguage: One job is spotting that something is broken; the other is carrying on regardless. ICMP does the spotting. This memo is about what TCP does next when the news is bad but might be out of date.

sections.title: Soft Errors, Hard Errors and the Codes That Signal Them
sections.content:
Network errors divide into soft and hard. Soft errors are transient network failures likely to be solved in the near term; hard errors reflect conditions unlikely to be solved in the near future.

The Host Requirements document lists the ICMP messages that indicate soft errors: Destination Unreachable codes 0 for network unreachable, 1 for host unreachable and 5 for source route failed; Time Exceeded codes 0 for time to live exceeded in transit and 1 for fragment reassembly time exceeded; and Parameter Problem. ICMPv6 did not exist when that document was written, but the same idea can be extrapolated to it: Destination Unreachable codes 0 for no route to destination and 3 for address unreachable; Time Exceeded codes 0 for hop limit exceeded in transit and 1 for fragment reassembly time exceeded; and Parameter Problem codes 0 for an erroneous header field encountered, 1 for an unrecognized next header type encountered and 2 for an unrecognized IPv6 option encountered.

When a network failure is not signalled to the sending host, for instance because a gateway corrupts packets, TCP's fault recovery action is to repeatedly retransmit the data until it is acknowledged or the connection times out. When an ICMP error message referring to an ongoing connection does arrive, the IP layer passes it up to the TCP instance, and TCP's reaction depends on the type of error.

For a hard error, compliant TCP implementations simply abort the connection, whatever state it is in. The Host Requirements document says TCP should abort on hard errors, on the premise that such conditions will not change in the near term, so there is no point trying to recover. The document notes that virtually none of the current implementations follow that advice, and do not abort the connection when a hard error arrives for a connection in any of the synchronized states.

For a soft error, TCP repeatedly retransmits until the data is acknowledged or the connection times out, and the sender may record the information for possible later use. The Host Requirements document says TCP must not abort on soft errors, on the premise that they are transient and one of the retransmissions will succeed. When the connection timer expires and a soft error had been received earlier, TCP can use that information to give the user a more specific error message. This reaction exploits a valuable feature of the Internet, that for many network failures the network can be dynamically reconstructed without any disruption of the endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: A soft error is a road closed for now; a hard error is a road gone for good. The old rules said to wait out a soft error and try again, because the network often fixes itself. The standard tells TCP to abort on a hard error, though almost no implementation actually does that either.

sections.title: The Problem: Waiting Minutes at the Wrong Door
sections.content:
Consider an application on a local host trying to reach a destination whose name resolves to several IP addresses. The application will usually cycle through the list until one succeeds. Suppose some, but not all, of the addresses in the returned list are permanently unreachable, and that a permanently unreachable address is first in the list: the application will try it first and block waiting for a timeout before trying an alternative.

If the unreachability is not signalled to the sending host at all, there is very little that can be done other than to repeatedly retransmit the SYN segment and wait for the TCP connection timer, or an application timeout, to be triggered. But even when unreachability is signalled by an intermediate router with an ICMP soft error, the local TCP will still repeatedly retransmit the SYN segment until the connection timer expires, in the hope that the error is transient. The Host Requirements document says that timer must be large enough to allow retransmission of the SYN segment for at least 3 minutes, so the application would spend several minutes on each unreachable address. Such long delays between connection-establishment attempts are inappropriate for interactive applications such as the Web. There is no single definition of a transient error, and how long to persist in the face of failure is a trade-off. It is worth noting that trying the addresses in series is not the only possible approach: an application could try several addresses in parallel until one succeeds, which would avoid the long delays.

A scenario where this happens regularly is dual-stack nodes with IPv6 enabled by default, deployed in IPv4 or mixed IPv4 and IPv6 environments, where the IPv6 connectivity does not exist. There are two variants, depending on whether the lack of connectivity is signalled. Where packets to the destination are silently dropped and no ICMPv6 errors are generated, there is little that can be done other than wait for the existing connection-timeout mechanism or an application timeout. Where a legacy node has no default routers and Neighbor Unreachability Detection fails for destinations assumed to be on-link, or where firewalls and other systems that enforce scope boundaries send ICMPv6 errors, the sending node is told about the unreachability, but compliant TCP will still not abort the connection on a soft error.
sections.plainLanguage: If the first house on your list is empty, waiting several minutes at its door before trying the second house is a waste of time. This bites hardest when a machine has IPv6 switched on but sits on a network with no IPv6 at all.

sections.title: Two Ways Deployed to Fix It
sections.content:
The fault recovery action might sensibly depend not only on the type of error reported but also on the state of the connection it is reported against. An error arriving in response to opening a new connection is probably caused by opening the connection improperly rather than by a transient network failure.

The first workaround follows that reasoning. A number of TCP implementations have modified their reaction to all ICMP soft errors and treat them as hard errors when they arrive for connections in the SYN-SENT or SYN-RECEIVED states. This has been implemented in the Linux kernel since version 2.0.0, released in 1996. The document notes that this change violates section 4.2.3.9 of the Host Requirements document, which says these messages indicate soft error conditions and that TCP must not abort the corresponding connection. The same treatment can also help with faulty middle-boxes: a host that receives a RST in response to a SYN carrying the ECN setup bits may resend the SYN with those bits cleared, and some faulty firewalls reject such requests with an ICMP soft error of type 3 code 0 or code 1 instead of a RST, so a system that treats soft errors as hard errors in the non-synchronized states could resend the SYN with the bits cleared.

The second workaround is more conservative: abort a connection in the SYN-SENT or SYN-RECEIVED states only after an ICMP soft error has been received a specified number of times and the SYN segment has been retransmitted more than a specified number of times. That needs two new TCP parameters, used only during connection establishment. MAXSYNREXMIT would specify how many times the SYN segment has to be retransmitted before a connection is aborted, and MAXSOFTERROR how many soft-error messages have to arrive first. Two state variables would store the counts: nsynrexmit, increased by one every time the SYN is retransmitted, and nsofterror, increased by one every time a soft error arrives, both starting at zero when the attempt begins. A connection in either of the two states would be aborted if nsynrexmit is greater than MAXSYNREXMIT and nsofterror is simultaneously greater than MAXSOFTERROR.

This gives the network more time to solve the connectivity problem than aborting on the first soft error, but depending on the values chosen it can still lead to long delays. BSD systems abort connections in the SYN-SENT or SYN-RECEIVED state when a second ICMP error is received and the SYN has been retransmitted more than three times, and they set up a connection-establishment timer that puts an upper limit on how long the attempt has to succeed, expiring after 75 seconds. This may be better than the three-minute timeout policy in the standard, but it may still be inappropriate for the problems in this document, and this more conservative approach has been implemented in BSD systems for more than ten years. The document also notes that the conservative approach is a generalized version of the first: with MAXSOFTERROR set to 1 and MAXSYNREXMIT set to zero, the two schemes are identical.
sections.plainLanguage: One way is to give up at the first "nobody home" sign. The careful way is to give up only after a few signs and a few more knocks, and to cap the total wait at 75 seconds. The careful way has been in the BSD systems for more than ten years.

sections.title: The Drawbacks of Giving Up Early
sections.content:
The document sets out three drawbacks of the non-standard modifications.

With non-deterministic transient network failures, a transient failure affects all the addresses returned by the name-to-address function, so every destination could be unreachable for a short period. A mobile system consisting of a cell and a repeater may pass through a tunnel and lose connectivity at the repeater, which sends ICMP soft errors back to the cell. A transient routing problem may make an intervening router drop a SYN segment and send an ICMP soft error back to the host. A SYN segment carrying data may get fragmented and some fragments lost, with the destination timing out the reassembly and sending an ICMP soft error back, although that scenario is unlikely because SYN segments rarely carry data in practice. In such cases the application could quickly cycle through all the IP addresses and return an error, when it could have let TCP retry a destination a few seconds later, by which time the transient problem would have disappeared. Here the modifications make TCP less robust than a standards-compliant implementation. Where a domain name maps to a single IP address, it might be better to try that address persistently according to the normal TCP rules, rather than aborting on the first soft error.

With deterministic transient network failures, upstream connectivity is instantiated only on an as-needed basis, so the connection that triggers the upstream connectivity can deterministically receive ICMP Destination Unreachables while that connectivity is being activated, and would then be aborted. Again, the modifications make TCP less robust.

With non-compliant network address translators, some NATs respond to an unsolicited inbound SYN segment with an ICMP soft error message. A system sending that unsolicited SYN and implementing the workaround will abort the connection on receiving the error, probably preventing TCP's simultaneous open from succeeding through the NAT. The document stresses that those NATs are not BEHAVE-compliant and should implement the corresponding requirement instead. Where such a NAT is deployed, TCP simultaneous opens could fail, which is undesirable but tolerable in many situations, since a number of host implementations of TCP do not support simultaneous opens at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Giving up too fast can backfire if the problem was only a short hiccup, like driving through a tunnel and losing signal for a moment. It also breaks a rare but real trick, where both ends open the connection at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modification described makes TCP abort a connection in the SYN-SENT or SYN-RECEIVED states when it receives an ICMP error indicating a soft error, and it could therefore be exploited to reset valid connections during the connection-establishment phase. The workaround makes TCP more vulnerable to attack, even if only slightly, though an attacker wishing to reset ongoing connections could already send any of the ICMP hard error messages in any connection state.

Generally, TCP backs off its retransmission timer each time it retransmits the SYN for the same connection. A TCP that implements the modification, trying the next address in the list on receiving an ICMP error, might end up injecting more packets into the network than if it had simply retried the same address a number of times. Compliant TCP implementations might already behave that way, for example by cycling through the list of IP addresses in response to RST segments, since there are currently no recommendations on limiting the rate at which SYN segments are sent to a specific destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster could send a fake "nobody home" note to make your computer give up on a connection it was opening. They could already send other fake notes, so this adds only a little risk.

viz.caption: THREE THINGS THAT CAN GO WRONG

items.title: A short outage everywhere
items.text: Every address fails at once, and the client gives up instead of retrying in a few seconds.

items.title: Outage on demand
items.text: The connection that switches the upstream path on gets the error and is killed.

items.title: A NAT that answers a SYN
items.text: Some NATs reply with an error, which stops a simultaneous open from working.
